events.label: Solver: design the algorithm
events.detail: Dynamic Programming (Fibonacci sequence) · claims O(n) time

data.key_insight: To reach step n, the last move must be either a 1-step from n-1 or a 2-step from n-2. Thus, the total ways to reach step n is the sum of ways to reach step n-1 and step n-2, which is the Fibonacci sequence.

steps.title: Handle base cases
steps.detail: If n is 1 or 2, directly return n since there are 1 way for 1 step and 2 ways for 2 steps.

steps.title: Iterate using two variables
steps.detail: Keep track of the number of ways for the previous two steps (representing ways(i-1) and ways(i-2)) and update them in a loop from 3 up to n.

steps.title: Return the result
steps.detail: Return the final computed number of ways for step n.

data.pattern_summary: Dynamic Programming breaks a problem down into overlapping subproblems that are solved recursively and reused, rather than recomputed.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The result for step n depends directly on the results of steps n-1 and n-2, creating overlapping subproblems.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers are used for searching pairs or subarrays in sequential data, not for counting recursive decision paths.

pattern_options.name: Greedy
pattern_options.feedback: Greedy choices make a locally optimal choice at each step without looking back, which fails here because we need the total count of all paths.

pattern_options.name: Backtracking
pattern_options.feedback: While recursion is used, backtracking is meant for finding all valid configurations or subsets rather than counting numeric values defined by a recurrence relation.

signals.phrase: number of distinct ways to reach the top
signals.hint: Implies you need to accumulate choices or paths from smaller sub-steps.

signals.phrase: climb either 1 or 2 steps at a time
signals.hint: Shows that each state branches into two smaller sub-states.

data.brute_force_idea: Use a recursive helper function to branch out by taking either 1 or 2 steps from the current position until you reach or exceed n.
data.brute_force_why: Every single call branches into two new recursive calls, creating a binary tree of height n.
data.bottleneck: The code recomputes the number of ways to reach the same step multiple times across different branches of the recursion tree.
bottleneck_hints: Draw out the recursive tree for n = 4 and look at which values are computed more than once.
Notice how many times the function calculates the ways to reach a smaller step like current = 2.
Ask yourself if you really need to recalculate a subproblem if you already solved it earlier.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force solution recomputes the same step combinations repeatedly by exploring every path recursively. The optimized dynamic programming approach removes this bottleneck by building solutions iteratively from the bottom up. Instead of storing all previous results, it only keeps track of the last two values since each step count depends solely on the two preceding ones.

derivation.note: The loop runs from 3 to n, executing roughly n times.
A single addition of two numbers.

data.time_summary: Lines 3 through 8 take constant time. The loop on line 10 runs n - 2 times, and the inner lines 11-13 take constant O(1) time per iteration. As shown by the measured evidence, doubling n doubles the total step count (e.g., n=16 takes 62 steps, n=32 takes 126 steps), confirming a linear O(n) time complexity.
data.space_summary: The algorithm only uses a fixed number of scalar variables (prev_two, prev_one, current) regardless of the input size n. Thus, the extra memory used is O(1).
data.takeaway: When a recursive solution recalculates overlapping subproblems like Fibonacci sequences, replace recursion with an iterative approach that stores only the required historical state variables.
mistakes: Using recursion without memoization, which leads to exponential O(2^n) time complexity.
Allocating an entire array or list to store all previous step counts when only the last two values are needed, wasting space.
Off-by-one errors in the loop range, causing the code to miss edge cases for small values of n like 1 or 2.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: The algorithm computes the number of distinct ways to climb n stairs by recognizing that the total ways to reach step n is the sum of ways to reach n-1 and n-2. This forms the Fibonacci sequence, which we can compute iteratively in linear time and constant space.
data.intuition: Imagine climbing a staircase where each step is a stone. To step onto stone n, your previous step must have been either stone n-1 (taking 1 step) or stone n-2 (taking 2 steps). Therefore, the number of ways to reach stone n is simply the sum of the ways to reach those two previous stones.

flow_nodes.label: Check n <= 2
flow_nodes.detail: If n is 1 or 2, return n immediately.

flow_nodes.label: Initialize variables
flow_nodes.detail: Set prev_two = 1 and prev_one = 2 for base cases.

flow_nodes.label: Loop 3 to n
flow_nodes.detail: Iterate from step 3 up to n.

flow_nodes.label: Compute current
flow_nodes.detail: current = prev_one + prev_two, then shift pointers.

flow_nodes.label: Return result
flow_nodes.detail: Return prev_one as the total ways to reach step n.

pitfalls: Returning n for all inputs without handling base cases correctly.
Off-by-one errors in the loop range.
Using O(n) extra space for an array when only the last two values are needed.
